Problem 1

  1. Find the prediction equation for log(π1/π2)log(π1/π2). [10 pts]

given that we use j = 1, 2, 3 to denote Yes, Undecided, N. The model gives us

log(π1/π3)=1.301−0.419∗1(Male)+0.342∗1(White)log(π1/π3)=1.301−0.419∗1(Male)+0.342∗1(White)
and
log(π2/π3)=−0.653−0.105∗1(Male)+0.271∗1(White)log(π2/π3)=−0.653−0.105∗1(Male)+0.271∗1(White)

log(π1/π2)=log(π1/π3)−log(π2/π3)log(π1/π2)=log⁡(π1/π3)−log(π2/π3)

log(π1/π2)=−1.712+−0.313(Male)+0.071∗1(White)log⁡(π1/π2)=−1.712+−0.313(Male)+0.071∗1(White)

library(nnet)
library(readr)
Data <- read_table("D:/Documents/BioStatistics/Belief Count.txt", 
    col_types = cols(Race = col_factor(levels = c("White", 
        "Black")), Gender = col_factor(levels = c("Male", 
        "Female")), Belief = col_factor(levels = c("No", 
        "Yes", "Undecided"))))

Data <- within(Data, Belief <- relevel(Belief, ref = "No"))
options(contrasts = c("contr.SAS", "contr.poly"))
model <- multinom(Belief ~ Gender + Race, data = Data, weights = Count, trace = FALSE)

# Output results
summary(model)

for π2/π3π2/π3 undecided vs no the log odds =-0.6530 (intercept) - 0.1051 (GenderMale) = -0.7581

the positive ratio in π1π1 suggests that π1>π3π1>π3 but the negative ratio for π2π2 shows that π2<π3π2<π3 and therefore π1>π3>π2π1>π3>π2

The saturated model has more paramaters compared to the main effects model and as such the degree of freedom represents the difference in parameters between them. Saturated model has 8 while the main effect has 6 the difference is 2.

comparing the effect of gender on opinion we get a p-score of 0.027<0.050.027<0.05 which suggests that there is a statistically significant effect of gender on opinion outcomes.

mod.s<-multinom(Belief ~ Gender*Race, data = Data,
weights = Count, trace = F)

length(coefficients(mod.s))-length(coefficients(model))
## [1] 2
model$deviance-mod.s$deviance
## [1] 0.8538556
#main vs saturate
anova(model,mod.s, test = "Chisq")
##           Model Resid. df Resid. Dev   Test    Df  LR stat.   Pr(Chi)
## 1 Gender + Race        18   1547.453           NA        NA        NA
## 2 Gender * Race        16   1546.599 1 vs 2     2 0.8538556 0.6525107
#main - gender
anova(update(model,~.-Gender), model, test = "Chisq")
##           Model Resid. df Resid. Dev   Test    Df LR stat.    Pr(Chi)
## 1          Race        20   1554.646           NA       NA         NA
## 2 Gender + Race        18   1547.453 1 vs 2     2 7.192654 0.02742427

Problem 2

A multinomial logistic regression model predicts preference for U.S. President (Democrat, Republican, Independent) using annual income xx = $10,000). The model equations are:

log(π^Dπ^I)=3.3−0.2xlog⁡(π^Dπ^I)=3.3−0.2x
and
log(π^Rπ^I)=1.0+0.3xlog⁡(π^Rπ^I)=1.0+0.3x
 Plot π^Dπ^D, π^Rπ^R and π^Iπ^I

Let π^I=11+e3.3−0.2x+e1.0+0.3xπ^I=11+e3.3−0.2x+e1.0+0.3x, then:

π^D=e3.3−0.2x1+e3.3−0.2x+e1.0+0.3x,π^R=e1.0+0.3x1+e3.3−0.2x+e1.0+0.3xπ^D=e3.3−0.2x1+e3.3−0.2x+e1.0+0.3x,π^R=e1.0+0.3x1+e3.3−0.2x+e1.0+0.3x

x <- seq(0,10, by=0.01)
pi_I <-1/(exp(3.3-0.2*x) + exp(1.0+0.3*x) + 1)
pi_D <-exp(3.3-0.2*x)/(exp(3.3-0.2*x) + exp(1.0+0.3*x) + 1)
pi_R <-exp(1.0+0.3*x)/(exp(3.3-0.2*x) + exp(1.0+0.3*x) + 1)
plot(x, pi_I, ylim=c(0,1), ylab="Probs", xlab="Annual income", type="l")
lines(x,pi_D, col=2)
lines(x,pi_R, col=4)
legend("top", c("Indep","Dem", "Rep"), lty=c(1,1,1), col=c(1,2,4))

Problem 3

The following table refers to a clinical trial for the treatment of small-cell lung cancer. Patients were randomly assigned to two treatment groups. The sequential therapy administered the same combination of chemotherapeutic agents in each treatment cycle; the alternating therapy had three different combinations, alternating from cycle to cycle.

  1. Fit a cumulative logit model with main effects for treatment and gender. Interpret. (If you use functions lrm or polr, the weights option may be used, depending on how you organize the data. If the data is organized in the same way as the mental impairment example in the lecture, the weights option is not needed. If the counts of each combination of the three variables are contained in the data, the weights option should be the counts). [15 pts]
library(rms)
## Loading required package: Hmisc
## 
## Attaching package: 'Hmisc'
## The following objects are masked from 'package:dplyr':
## 
##     src, summarize
## The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
## 
##     format.pval, units
Therapy <- c("S", "A") # Therapy
Gender <- c("M", "F") # Gender
ResChem <- c(1:4) # response scores integers
Count <- c(28,45,29,26,4,12,5,2,41,44,20,20,12,7,3,1)
Data2=cbind(expand.grid( ResChem=ResChem ,Gender=Gender, Therapy=Therapy),
Count)
Data2
##    ResChem Gender Therapy Count
## 1        1      M       S    28
## 2        2      M       S    45
## 3        3      M       S    29
## 4        4      M       S    26
## 5        1      F       S     4
## 6        2      F       S    12
## 7        3      F       S     5
## 8        4      F       S     2
## 9        1      M       A    41
## 10       2      M       A    44
## 11       3      M       A    20
## 12       4      M       A    20
## 13       1      F       A    12
## 14       2      F       A     7
## 15       3      F       A     3
## 16       4      F       A     1
Data2$ResChem.original <- factor(Data2$ResChem)
levels(Data2$ResChem.original) <-c("1:PD","2:NC","3:PR","4:CR")
Data2$ResChem.original
##  [1] 1:PD 2:NC 3:PR 4:CR 1:PD 2:NC 3:PR 4:CR 1:PD 2:NC 3:PR 4:CR 1:PD 2:NC 3:PR
## [16] 4:CR
## Levels: 1:PD 2:NC 3:PR 4:CR
Data2$ResChem.rev <- factor(5-Data2$ResChem)
levels(Data2$ResChem.rev) <- c("CR:1","PR:2","NC:3","PD:4")
Data2$ResChem.rev
##  [1] PD:4 NC:3 PR:2 CR:1 PD:4 NC:3 PR:2 CR:1 PD:4 NC:3 PR:2 CR:1 PD:4 NC:3 PR:2
## [16] CR:1
## Levels: CR:1 PR:2 NC:3 PD:4
mod.lrm <- lrm(ResChem.rev ~ Gender + Therapy, weights=Count, data = Data2)

  1. What are P(Y ≤≤ “No Change”) and P(Y ≤≤ “Partial Remission”) for a male receiving sequential therapy? What are P(Y = “No Change”) and P(Y =“Partial Remission”)? [10 pts]

Given that:

logit(P(≤j))=αj+βtherapy(Alternative)+βgender(Female)logit(P(≤j))=αj+βtherapy(Alternative)+βgender(Female)
our cumulative probabilities are
P(Y≤j)=exp(logit)/1+exp(logit)P(Y≤j)=exp(logit)/1+exp(logit)
 P(Y≤PR)=exp(1.3001)/(1+exp(1.3001))=0.7863P(Y≤PR)=exp(1.3001)/(1+exp(1.3001))=0.7863

P(Y≤NC)=exp(0.2492)/(1+exp(0.2492))=0.5619P(Y≤NC)=exp(0.2492)/(1+exp(0.2492))=0.5619

P(Y≤PD)=exp(−1.3180)/(1+exp(−1.3180))=0.2111P(Y≤PD)=exp(−1.3180)/(1+exp(−1.3180))=0.2111

P(Y=NC)=P(Y≤NC)−P(Y≤PD)=0.562−0.211=0.351P(Y=NC)=P(Y≤NC)−P(Y≤PD)=0.562−0.211=0.351

P(Y=PR)=P(Y≤PR)−P(Y≤NoChange)=0.786−0.562=0.224P(Y=PR)=P(Y≤PR)−P(Y≤NoChange)=0.786−0.562=0.224

newdata <- data.frame(expand.grid(Therapy = c("S", "A"),
Gender = c("M", "F")))
newdata <- cbind(newdata,predict(mod.lrm,newdata,type="fitted"))
newdata

  1. Fit the model that also contains an interaction term. Interpret. Does it fit better? (The deviance of a lrm object A can be obtained as A$deviance[2])[15 pts]

We will use a likelihood ratio test to compare the model fits, we get a p-value of 0.31 which means we do not haave sufficient evidence to reject the null hypothesis and we may conclude that there is no statistical difference between the two models.

fit.lrm.int <- lrm(ResChem.rev ~ Gender*Therapy, weights=Count, data = Data2)
## Warning in lrm(ResChem.rev ~ Gender * Therapy, weights = Count, data = Data2):
## currently weights are ignored in model validation and bootstrapping lrm fits
fit.lrm.int

## 
## lrm(formula = ResChem.rev ~ Gender * Therapy, data = Data2, weights = Count)

## max |deriv| 1e-06    Pr(> chi2) 0.0075    R2(3,274.7)0.032    gamma   0.236    
##                                             Brier    0.135    tau-a   0.121    
##

## y>=PR:2               1.3452 0.1906  7.06  <0.0001 
## y>=NC:3               0.2957 0.1678  1.76  0.0781  
## y>=PD:4              -1.2757 0.1844 -6.92  <0.0001 
## Gender=F              0.2742 0.3873  0.71  0.4790  
## Therapy=A             0.4881 0.2305  2.12  0.0342  
## Gender=F * Therapy=A  0.5904 0.5792  1.02  0.3080
G2 <- mod.lrm$deviance[2]-fit.lrm.int$deviance[2]
df <- length(coef(fit.lrm.int))-length(coef(mod.lrm))
pchisq(G2,df, lower=F)
## [1] 0.3062483
